2	
3	A daily journaling app with an AI **Journaling Assistant** that walks you through
4	a structured reflection — up to 10 topics per session — and produces a summarized
5	journal entry. This is a ground-up rebuild of the original emotely (a shipped

16	## Decisions
17	
18	The load-bearing decisions and their rationale live in [`docs/adr/`](docs/adr/):
19

21	2. [Tools-first harness](docs/adr/0002-tools-first-harness.md) — tool calls, not prompted JSON
22	3. [Model gateway + cost ceiling](docs/adr/0003-model-gateway-and-cost-ceiling.md) — provider-agnostic, cheap-model constraint

30	## Architecture
31	
32	Monorepo. Two apps that share one contract, plus Supabase (data/auth) and
33	PostHog (analytics + the self-driving loop).
34	
35	```
36	emotely/
37	├─ apps/
38	│  ├─ agent/      TypeScript · Vercel AI SDK agent loop · deploys to Vercel
39	│  │             tools: ask_topic / record_answer / complete_session
40	│  │             evals/ — offline fixtures → cost + quality (CI gate)
41	│  └─ app/        Flutter (iOS + Android) · renders one native widget per tool call
42	├─ packages/
43	│  └─ contract/   the tool-call schema — single source of truth for both sides
44	└─ README.md
45	```
46	
47	### Why a monorepo
48	
49	The agent and the app are two halves of one product joined by **one contract**:
50	the agent emits tool calls, the app renders a native widget per call. That shared
51	schema (`packages/contract`) must never drift between producer and consumer — in a
52	monorepo a schema change plus both sides move in one atomic, CI-verified commit.
53	Solo founder → one CI, one release story, one front door. Both repos are public
54	anyway, so the usual "keep one half private" argument doesn't apply.
55	
56	Tooling stays boring: pnpm workspaces for the TS side, Flutter's own tooling for
57	`apps/app`, path-filtered GitHub Actions. No Nx/Turbo/Bazel.
58	
59	### The stack
60	
61	| Layer | Choice | Why |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| **Client** | Flutter, iOS + Android only (no web) | Native GenUI story; VGV/Flutter-community audience |
64	| **Agent runtime** | TypeScript · Vercel AI SDK · Vercel | Tools-first agent loop, streaming, the AI-eng showcase |
65	| **Model access** | Gateway (Vercel AI Gateway **or** OpenRouter) | Swap models via config; benchmark cheap models on real sessions |
66	| **Data + auth** | Supabase (Postgres + Auth) | Fresh schema, no Firebase baggage |
67	| **Observability** | PostHog (full bundle, see below) | LLM obs, flags, experiments, error tracking, Max AI |
68	| **Subscriptions** | RevenueCat | Known quantity from the original app |
69	| **License** | MIT, both apps | Portfolio-friendly, maximally reusable |
70	
71	### Tool-calling replaces the old JSON hack
72	
73	The original assistant ran on the Firebase GenAI Chatbot extension: a ~2KB prompt
74	that *begged* the model to emit parseable JSON (`response` + `summary`), with a
75	"recovery prompt" retry when the JSON didn't parse. That's fighting the model.
76	
77	The rebuild gives the model **tools** instead:
78	
79	- `ask_topic(topic, input_type)` — `input_type ∈ text | color_picker | mood_slider | multi_select`; the client renders the matching native widget. **This is the generative UI.**
80	- `record_answer(topic, value)` — structured, validated tool args. No JSON-parsing prayer.
81	- `complete_session(summary)` — the summary is a validated tool argument, not parsed prose.
82	
83	The old `ColorText` / `ColorTextEditingController` feature becomes just one
84	`input_type` (`color_picker`).
85	
86	## PostHog — the "self-driving" layer
87	
88	Adopted day one (all free at our scale, ~0€ at 1k MAU):
89	
90	- **Product analytics** — `posthog_flutter` (app) + `posthog-node` (agent).
91	- **LLM observability** — `@posthog/ai` with `experimental_telemetry` on AI SDK
92	  calls → `$ai_generation` events (tokens, cost, latency, traces per model).
93	  **`privacyMode` ON** — journal text never leaves the device to PostHog; only
94	  metadata is captured. Non-negotiable for a journaling app.
95	- **Feature flags + experiments** — a flag payload `{ model, prompt }` drives
96	  **server-side model selection** in the agent, no deploy. PostHog's **LLM prompt
97	  experiments** auto-attribute cost + quality per variant.
98	- **Error tracking** — native PostHog exception tracking. **No Sentry.**
99	- **Max AI + anomaly alerts** — agentic analyst that watches AI-cost-per-user and
100	  session-completion and pings on drift. This is the self-driving watchdog.
101	- **Session replay + surveys** — deferred (replay only with mask-all-text, given
102	  sensitive journal content).
103	
104	**The self-driving loop:** PostHog flag hands the agent `{model, prompt}` →
105	`@posthog/ai` emits cost/latency per variant → LLM prompt experiment attributes
106	cost + quality per variant → Max AI / anomaly alerts flag drift. The product tunes
107	its own model choice; you get pinged instead of dashboard-staring.
108	
109	Set **billing limits / spike protection** per product on day one — a retry storm
110	must not surprise-bill.
111	
112	## Cost model (the hard constraint)
113	
114	A daily poweruser (~30 sessions/month, ~10 topics each) must cost **well under
115	50¢/month**, ideally a few cents, inside a 5€ sub with high margins.
116	
117	- Frontier models (Claude Sonnet/Opus) — **out**, blow the budget per session.
118	- Haiku-class — borderline (~$1.50–2.70/mo).
119	- **Gemini Flash-Lite / GLM-4.x-class** — a few cents to ~60¢/mo, and the only
120	  tier that hits "a few cents."
121	- **Prompt caching** on the static context prompt cuts session cost 3–5× — this
122	  matters more than the exact model.
123	- The task is narrow and well-specified (10 fixed topics, extract → summarize) —
124	  a cheap model with good tool-calling is enough. No frontier reasoning needed.
125	
126	Final model is chosen **empirically** at build time via the eval harness + a
127	PostHog LLM prompt experiment, not from memory.
128	
129	## Two layers of evaluation
130	
131	1. **Offline evals** (`apps/agent/evals/`) — deterministic fixtures replayed
132	   against each candidate model. The CI gate; catches regressions before ship.
133	   Seed from the original app's `promptfoo` conversation fixtures.
134	2. **Online experiment** (PostHog) — real sessions, real cost, live variant
135	   comparison. The self-driving loop.
136	
137	Offline proves *correct + cheap in the lab*; online proves *cheap + retained in
138	the wild*.
139	
140	## Build order
141	
142	1. **`apps/agent` skeleton** — Vercel AI SDK loop, the three tools, gateway wired,
143	   one cheap model hardcoded. Prove a full 10-topic session runs end-to-end via

146	   fixtures into `evals/`. CI gate: replay, assert correctness, measure cost per
147	   candidate.
148	3. **Benchmark** — run evals across GLM-4.x / Gemini Flash-Lite / Haiku; pick the
149	   cheapest that passes. Add prompt caching. Confirm poweruser cost. **Decide the
150	   gateway here** (OpenRouter has a dedicated PostHog install path; Vercel AI

152	4. **PostHog online** — `@posthog/ai` (privacyMode on), flag-driven model
153	   selection, first LLM prompt experiment.
154	5. **`apps/app`** — Flutter shell rendering a widget per tool call, Supabase auth +

157

167	## Legacy
168	
169	The original app lives at `~/dev/emotely-legacy` (Flutter + Firebase, sunset early

171	design, the `promptfoo` conversation fixtures, the `ColorText` idea, and the strong

On your second question — **where to keep tooling context so agents know it exists:**

[CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) is the discovery point — it's the one file every agent session loads automatically, so anything not reachable from there effectively doesn't exist for an agent. But it should stay short, so the pattern that fits this repo's existing convention (README → `docs/adr/`, `CONTEXT.md`):

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. Most repos have a single context:

/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md

├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

I've got everything I need for round 1 — including a find: the legacy context prompt survives in `~/dev/emotely-legacy/backend/extensions/firestore-genai-chatbot.env`, and it reveals that in the original app **topics were given to the assistant** (with per-topic format instructions and answer counts), not invented by the model. That shapes several questions below.

Here's the frontier — 9 independent decisions. Answers to these unblock the next round (contract details, state shape, model ID research).

---

❓ **Q1** - **Where do topics come from?**: The README says "up to 10 topics per session", ADR 0003 says "10 fixed topics". The legacy prompt was *handed* a topic set per date ("You will be given a set of topics... Each topic comes with instructions"). For the rebuild: (a) a fixed hardcoded topic list the agent walks through, (b) a configurable list passed into the session (per-user/per-date later), or (c) the model chooses topics freely? And is `ask_topic`'s `topic` argument then an enum from that list or a free string?

➡️ (b) with (a)'s content for now: the session loop takes a topic list as input, skeleton hardcodes one default list of 10. `topic` stays a free string in the contract (the list is session config, not schema) — enum would force a contract change per topic tweak.

❓ **Q2** - **How does the user's answer flow back?**: Two viable loop shapes. **(a) Client-executed tool:** `ask_topic` is a tool the *client* answers — its tool result carries the raw widget value back to the model, which then calls `record_answer` with the normalized, validated value. **(b) Plain chat turn:** the widget answer comes back as a user message; the model calls `record_answer` from it. (a) is the AI SDK generative-UI idiom and keeps the transcript structured end-to-end; (b) is simpler but re-introduces prose-parsing at the seam.

➡️ (a). `ask_topic` = client-side tool (no `execute` on the agent; the driver/Flutter app supplies the result), `record_answer` = server-side tool that validates and stores. This makes the CLI driver an honest stand-in for the Flutter client.

❓ **Q3** - **How is `record_answer.value` typed?**: (a) A discriminated union per input type — `text` → string, `mood_slider` → number in a fixed range, `color_picker` → hex string, `multi_select` → string array. (b) Just a string, interpret later.

➡️ (a). The contract is the single source of truth the Flutter side renders against; a stringly-typed `value` would smuggle the old JSON-parsing problem back in through the side door.

❓ **Q4** - **One answer per topic, or several?**: The legacy prompt had "number of answers required" per topic and examples show it collecting *multiple* answers ("What else did you learn?"). CONTEXT.md currently implies one ask/one record per topic. Does v1 allow multiple `record_answer` calls per topic?

➡️ Allow multiple: the contract doesn't forbid it (same `topic` on repeated calls just appends), and the topic list input carries an optional per-topic hint like the legacy design. Costs nothing in schema, matches how the assistant actually behaved.

❓ **Q5** - **Runtime shape for #2**: Local-only session loop invoked by the CLI driver, or also an HTTP endpoint deployed to Vercel now?

➡️ Local only. The loop is a plain async function (`runSession(config, io)`); the CLI driver is one consumer, the Vercel route becomes a second consumer when the Flutter client lands (#6). No deploy in #2.

❓ **Q6** - **What is the CLI driver?**: (a) Interactive — you journal in the terminal via stdin, real dogfooding from day one. (b) Scripted — canned answers, deterministic run.

➡️ (a) interactive. Deterministic replay is exactly what issue #3 (offline evals) builds — building a scripted driver now would duplicate it a week early. And "I journal with it daily" starts working at #2 instead of #6.

❓ **Q7** - **Which gateway to wire first?**: ADR 0003 defers the *final* vendor to issue #4, but the skeleton needs one wired now: Vercel AI Gateway or OpenRouter?

➡️ Vercel AI Gateway. Native to the AI SDK (model is a `'provider/model'` string — the "swappable via config" criterion becomes a single env var), one key, you deploy to Vercel anyway. OpenRouter gets its fair fight in #4 as the ADR intends.

❓ **Q8** - **System prompt source**: Adapt the legacy CONTEXT prompt (found it — it encodes real learned behavior: one topic at a time, the off-topic-redirect discipline, tone/emoji, treat off-topic remarks as data for the current topic) or write a minimal fresh one?

➡️ Adapt legacy. Strip everything that existed to serve the JSON hack and the "topics given as text" mechanism (tools replace both); keep the behavioral core. It's also the prompt the #3 eval fixtures were written against, so continuity helps there.

❓ **Q9** - **Session end + guardrails**: A session ends when the model calls `complete_session`. What about: the user saying "I'm done" mid-session (model should skip remaining topics and complete), and a runaway loop (model never completes)? Also: is the test story for #2 TDD with the AI SDK's mock language model, with the live 10-topic run as the manual acceptance check — or do you want live-model assertions in CI already?

➡️ User can end early → prompt instructs model to call `complete_session` with what it has. Hard cap via the SDK's step limit (~3 steps per topic + slack) as the runaway guard. TDD with mock model in CI; live run stays manual until #3 makes it an eval.

# Legacy emotely: question sets & input types

## 1. The set concept: `JournalQuestionSet`

Not "topic set" or "template" — the code says **question set**. The word "topic" appears *only* in the LLM context prompt in `firestore-genai-chatbot.env`; there is zero occurrence of "topic" in the Dart codebase. The app calls them questions.

Three-layer model, and the split matters:

**`JournalQuestion`** — `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/journal_question.dart`
```dart
required String id;                          // Firestore doc id
required Translations localizations;         // Map<String,String>, lang code -> question text
required JournalQuestionAnswerType type;     // the input type
@Default(<String>[]) List<String> tags;       // DEAD — never read anywhere
int? minAnswers;                              // null => treated as 1
int? maxAnswers;                              // DEAD — never enforced anywhere
```
`Translations = Map<String, String>` (`/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/typedefs.dart:10`). Localization falls back to `localizations[languageCode] ?? first entry`, else throws `MissingLocalizationException`.

**`JournalQuestionSet`** — `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/journal_question_set.dart`
```dart
required String id;
required Translations name;
Translations? description;
bool? isPremium;
@Default(<JournalQuestion>[]) List<JournalQuestion> questions;  // hydrated, ordered
```

**`JournalQuestionSetDto`** — `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/dtos/journal_question_set_dto.dart` — this is the **Firestore wire shape**. Same fields but `List<String> questionIds` instead of embedded questions. `toJournalQuestionSet()` joins ids against a question map; **missing ids are silently dropped** (logged as a warning, set still returned shorter than declared). Ordering is the order of `questionIds`.

### Where sets live: Firestore, not assets

Four collections, all read at runtime (`firestore.rules`):
- `question-sets/{setId}` — public sets, world-readable to any authed user
- `journal-questions/{questionId}` — public questions
- `users/{uid}/question-sets/{setId}` — private sets
- `users/{uid}/journal-questions/{questionId}` — private questions

Providers: `public_question_sets_provider.dart:61`, `public_questions_provider.dart:14`, `private_question_sets_service.dart:47`, `private_questions_service.dart:42`. Selection resolves private-first, then public (`selected_question_set_provider.dart:59-69`), defaulting to `KT9cr1mEoilCTNC6o3mK`.

One set is **hardcoded**: `legacyQuestionSet` in `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/legacy.dart` — 10 questions, same id `KT9cr1mEoilCTNC6o3mK`, used as the `@Default` for `JournalEntry.questionSet` so pre-question-set entries still render. It's the only place you can see a full concrete set without a live Firestore.

### Could users author their own sets? **No — the machinery exists but is unreachable.**

`PrivateQuestionSetsService.putQuestionSet` / `deleteQuestionSet` / `getNewQuestionSetId` and the `PrivateQuestionsService` equivalents are fully implemented, and Firestore rules allow the writes. But grepping for callers across `app/lib`, `feature/`, and `widgetbook/` returns **nothing** outside the service files themselves. `question_sets_view.dart` has no create/edit/delete affordance — `QuestionSetsController` only exposes `setSelectedQuestionSet`, `handleCheckout`, `refresh`. So in shipped behavior: pick from predefined sets only. Private sets were a half-built feature (backend + service layer done, UI never landed).

Also worth flagging for contract v1: `question_sets_controller.dart:33-52` has premium filtering commented out with `// SUBSCRIPTION SALES DISCONTINUED. Code for demo purposes only`.

## 2. How a set got into the model context

The chosen set is **denormalized onto the journal entry**, then rendered to text at session start. Two steps:

**Step 1 — freeze the set onto the entry.** `journaling_setup_controller.dart:118-138`: on pressing the journaling-assistant button, `_updateEntryWithSelectedQuestionSet()` does `journalEntry.copyWith(questionSet: questionSet)` and writes it. The entry stores the **entire hydrated set including full question objects**, not a reference — so past entries survive set edits.

**Step 2 — render to a system message.** `journaling_assistant_controller.dart:110-123`: on build, if the chat collection is empty, send an initialization prompt.

`_createQuestionsString` (`:307-319`) is the composition point:
```dart
return '${question.id}: $questionText - $typeInstructions\n\n';
```
joined with `'\n'`. The `typeInstructions` come from `JournalingAssistantJournalQuestionAnswerTypeExtension.toLocalizedInstructions` (`/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/ui/pages/journaling_assistant/extensions/journaling_assistant_journal_question_answer_type_extension.dart`) — a pure switch on the enum to a localized string. **These are per-type constants, not per-question.** `minAnswers` never reaches the prompt.

The wrapper is a localization template, `journalingAssistantInitialPrompt` (`app_localizations_en.dart:966-974`), 5 positional args:
```
Journaling history:
{history}

The user's name is {name}. Please talk to them in english.

This conversation is about the journal entry for {entryDate}.

Now is {nowIso8601}.

Collect the following information:
{questionsString}
```
History is built by `_createJournalingHistoryString` (`:282-299`) as `{date}:\n{questionId}: {localizedQuestion} - {answersJoined}`.

Sent via `JournalingAssistantServiceImpl.sendMessage(prompt, isSystemMessage: true)`, which **prefixes the literal string `'System prompt: '`** and sets `isSystemMessage: true` on the doc (`journaling_assistant_service.dart:76-82`). The Firebase GenAI chatbot extension picks it up from `users/{userID}/journalEntries/{date}/chat`, prepends the static `CONTEXT` env var, and writes back `response`.

So the env prompt's "Each topic comes with instructions on the format and number of answers required" refers to exactly these five localized strings.

Trust the localization file.

## 3. The five input types

Enum `JournalQuestionAnswerType` (`journal_question.dart:10-21`). The user's recollection maps correctly but the names differ: "multi-answer" is `text`, "long text" is `longtext`.

| Enum | JSON (`type`) | Union tag (`answerType`) | Class | Answer field & type | Multi? | Validation | Prompt instruction (EN) |

All in `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/journal_content.dart` (a freezed union, `@Freezed(unionKey: 'answerType')`). Each variant carries an `@Assert` that the embedded `question.type` matches its variant.

One complete run of the Journaling Assistant: the assistant walks the user

One thing the assistant asks about within a session — a concrete question text

How a question is answered, and therefore which native widget the client renders

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification — "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists — and survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams — where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

When the shape of that interface is itself in question — how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose — use the `/codebase-design` skill for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled** — mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological** — the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth — a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing** — writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead — one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

## Code sketches (all behavior probe-verified against `ai@7.0.70`)

**(a) Client-side tool — caller supplies the result.** I ran this; I did not infer it. With no `execute`, the loop halts at `finishReason: "tool-calls"` and exposes `toolCalls`. No error is thrown.

```ts
import { generateText, tool, isStepCount, type ModelMessage } from 'ai';
import { z } from 'zod';

const askQuestion = tool({
  description: 'Ask the user a question',
  inputSchema: z.object({ question: z.string() }),
  // no execute => client-side; loop stops and hands you the call
});

const messages: ModelMessage[] = [{ role: 'user', content: 'hi' }];

while (true) {
  const r = await generateText({
    model: 'zai/glm-4.7-flash',
    tools: { askQuestion },
    stopWhen: isStepCount(10),
    messages,
  });
  messages.push(...r.response.messages);
  if (r.finishReason !== 'tool-calls') { console.log(r.text); break; }

  for (const tc of r.toolCalls) {
    const answer = await promptUser(tc.input.question); // your CLI
    messages.push({
      role: 'tool',
      content: [{
        type: 'tool-result',
        toolCallId: tc.toolCallId,
        toolName: tc.toolName,
        output: { type: 'json', value: { answer } }, // discriminated union!
      }],
    });
  }
}
```

`output` **must** be `{type:'json'|'text', value}`. Passing a raw object (the v5 style) throws `InvalidPromptError` — I verified this failure mode explicitly.
Docs: https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/tools-and-tool-calling

## Creating API Keys

You can create a key from the dashboard, the Vercel CLI, or the Vercel API.

### Dashboard Method
Go to the AI Gateway API Keys page and click Create key, then name and create the key. Copy the key value immediately (you cannot retrieve it again) and save it as AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.

The CLI command format is: `vercel ai-gateway api-keys create --name <NAME> --budget <DOLLARS> --refresh-period <PERIOD>`
